articles.title: The Color No One Could See
articles.dek: An eighteenth-century astronomer aimed a thermometer at empty space beside a rainbow and found a kind of light no human eye had ever detected — which is exactly how Paul says God's wisdom works.
articles.quote: God's wisdom isn't hidden because it's dim. It takes a different kind of sight to see it — and God freely gives that sight to anyone who asks.
articles.illustration: William Herschel's discovery of infrared light
articles.body:
In 1800, the astronomer William Herschel set up a simple experiment in his garden. He passed sunlight through a glass prism, splitting it into the familiar rainbow band — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet. Then he did something no one had thought to try. He laid thermometers along the spectrum, one under each color, to measure how much heat each band carried. Violet was cool. Red was warmer. And then, almost as an afterthought, he placed one more thermometer just past the red edge, in the space where the light seemed to end and the eye saw nothing at all.

That thermometer read the highest temperature of them all.

Herschel had found a kind of light that no human eye could register — real, measurable, full of energy — sitting in plain sight the whole time. He called it "invisible light." Today we call it infrared. It hadn't been absent. It had simply been beyond the range of the instrument most people trust the most: their own eyes. You needed a different kind of sensor to detect it. Once you had one, the proof was overwhelming.

Paul makes almost the identical claim about the wisdom of God — and he makes it to a city that trusted its eyes, and its ears, more than almost any city in the ancient world.

Corinth ran on rhetoric. Traveling teachers called sophists moved through the marketplace like celebrities, prized for how cleverly they could argue, how polished their delivery was, how impressive they sounded on a public stage. The church at Corinth had absorbed that culture. Believers were ranking their favorite teachers the way people rank favorite speakers today, and some were quietly asking why Paul's preaching didn't sound more like the professionals.

Paul's answer is startling. He agrees that there is a wisdom he speaks — "a message of wisdom among the mature" (1 Corinthians 2:6) — but he says plainly that it is not the wisdom Corinth was trained to recognize. It isn't sharper logic or better delivery. It is, he says, "God's wisdom, a mystery that has been hidden and that God destined for our glory before time began" (2:7). Then he quotes an old promise from Isaiah, almost as if daring his readers to believe it: "What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no mind has conceived, the things God has prepared for those who love him" (2:9).

No eye. No ear. No mind. Read fast, that sounds like God's wisdom is simply out of reach — dim, distant, unreachable by ordinary people. But Paul's very next sentence flips the whole picture.

"These are the things God has revealed to us by his Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." — 1 Corinthians 2:10 (NIV)

The wisdom was never dim. It just required a different instrument than the ones Corinth was so proud of.

Notice how carefully Paul builds the case. He asks who can know a person's inner thoughts except that person's own spirit (2:11) — an ordinary observation anyone would grant. Then he applies the same logic to God: "no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God" (2:11). And he says believers have received exactly that Spirit, "that we may understand what God has freely given us" (2:12). This is worth sitting with. Paul isn't saying spiritual truth is for an elite few with rare intellectual gifts. He's saying it was never an intelligence problem in the first place. It was a sensor problem. "The person without the Spirit does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God... they are discerned only through the Spirit" (2:14). You cannot out-think your way into it, the same way you cannot out-stare your way into seeing infrared. You need the right kind of sight, and that sight is a gift, not an achievement.

This is such good news for anyone who has ever felt outmatched — by a sharper debater, a more polished preacher, a louder voice online insisting they've reasoned their way past faith. Paul isn't asking Corinth to become smarter than the sophists. He's telling them they already possess something the cleverest sophist in the city does not. He lands the whole argument on one breathtaking sentence: "But we have the mind of Christ" (2:16). Not we are working toward it. Not we hope to earn it someday. We have it. Present tense. Already given.

Herschel needed a thermometer because the human eye was never built to detect infrared — and that was no defect in the eye. It simply wasn't designed for that job. In the same way, unaided human reasoning was never built to fully register the deep things of God — and that isn't a flaw in your mind. It's simply not the instrument for that particular kind of seeing. God supplied a better one: his own Spirit, given to "those who love him" (2:9), searching "the deep things of God" (2:10) on your behalf and inside you.

So here's something practical to carry out of this passage. The next time you open your Bible and a verse feels flat, or a truth about God feels just out of reach, try changing instruments before you assume the light isn't there. Instead of reading harder, pause and ask the Spirit — plainly, out loud if you want — to show you what's past the edge of what your own reasoning can pick up. That's not a lesser way to study Scripture. According to Paul, it's the only way anyone has ever truly seen it. The wisdom was never too dim for you. You just needed the sight that was already promised, and already yours.

articles.title: If Only There Were Someone
articles.dek: Job cried out for someone to stand between him and God, not knowing he had just described the very thing that would one day save him.
articles.quote: Job didn't need someone to explain his suffering. He needed someone to stand between him and it.
articles.illustration: Henry Dunant founding the Red Cross
articles.body:
On a scorching June afternoon in 1859, a Swiss businessman named Henry Dunant rode into the Italian town of Solferino hoping to get a business permit signed by the emperor. Instead he found forty thousand dead and wounded men scattered across the hills, French and Italian soldiers tangled together with Austrians, left where they fell because the armies had already marched on to keep killing each other elsewhere. Dunant forgot about his permit. He gathered the women of the nearby village of Castiglione and organized them to carry water, bandages, and bread to every wounded man they could find, whichever uniform he wore. Their rule was simple: tutti fratelli, all are brothers. Dunant himself moved back and forth between the French and the Austrians, an outsider with no rank and no side, the one man both armies would let near their wounded. Out of that single terrible afternoon came an idea that became the Red Cross.

What made Dunant useful was not medical skill. It was that he belonged to neither side, so both sides could trust his hands.

Job, sitting in ashes on the far side of tragedy, was aching for exactly that kind of person.

Night after night, Job cannot sleep. "When I lie down I think, how long before I get up? The night drags on, and I toss and turn until dawn," he says in chapter 7 (Job 7:4). His skin breaks out in sores and heals over with dirt, then cracks open again (Job 7:5). He is so worn down he begs God to simply look away for a moment. "Will you never look away from me, nor let me alone even for an instant?" (Job 7:19). That is a man asking for nothing more than a breath of space.

Into that exhaustion walks his friend Bildad, in chapter 8, with a tidy little sermon: God does not pervert justice, Bildad says, so if Job's children died, they must have sinned, and if Job would only seek God earnestly, he would be restored (Job 8:3-6). It is the kind of comfort that sounds reasonable in a seminar and lands like a slap beside a grave.

Job answers in chapter 9, and what he says is remarkable. He does not argue with Bildad's theology. He half agrees with it. "Indeed, I know that this is true," he says. "But how can mere mortals prove their innocence before God?" (Job 9:2). Job knows God is just. He also knows he cannot get a fair hearing, not because God is unjust, but because the two of them are not equals. "Though I were innocent, my mouth would condemn me," he says. "Though I were blameless, it would pronounce me guilty" (Job 9:20). He is too small, too rattled, too outmatched to make his case standing alone in front of that much power.

And then Job says something that stops the whole book for a moment.

He is not a mere mortal like me that I might answer him, that we might confront each other in court. If only there were someone to mediate between us, someone to bring us together, someone to remove God's rod from me, so that his terror would frighten me no more.

That is Job 9:32-34. Read it slowly. Job wants to plead his case, but there is no courtroom where a suffering man and an infinite God can stand as equals. He needs a third party. Someone who can put one hand on Job's shoulder and one hand toward God, someone both sides would trust, the way both armies at Solferino trusted a stranger who owed allegiance to neither.

Job didn't need someone to explain his suffering. He needed someone to stand between him and it.

Here is what's worth noticing: Job asks for this mediator as a wish, almost a lament, because as far as he can tell, no such person exists. "If only," he says. A few lines later the ache turns to resignation: "as it now stands with me, I cannot" speak up without fear (Job 9:35). Job names the exact shape of what he needs and then watches it slip through his fingers, because in his moment of history, it does not yet exist.

It is worth sitting with how far off that answer still was. Centuries would pass. An entire history of priests and sacrifices and prophets would unfold, all of it circling the same problem Job put into words in his grief: how does a small, frightened person get a fair hearing with a holy God? And then, long after Job's story was written down, a letter would go out from a man named Paul with this line in it: "For there is one God and one mediator between God and mankind, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 2:5). The very word Job used, the very ache Job named, gets answered by name.

Job cried out for someone to lay a steadying hand on both sides of an impossible gap. He did not live to see who that would be. We do.

That changes something practical about how we're allowed to pray. Job held himself back in verse 35 because he was afraid to speak freely. Many of us do the same thing, quietly assuming our complaints, our confusion, our unedited grief are too much to bring straight to God, that we need to clean them up first or route them through someone more qualified. But if the mediator Job longed for has already arrived, we no longer have to negotiate access. We do not need a stranger's neutral hand to broker a truce, because the mediator himself has already stood in the gap, and unlike Dunant, he is not neutral out of duty. He is for us, completely, on purpose.

This does not mean every hard question gets answered on the spot. Job's did not, not for many more chapters, and even then not quite the way he expected. But the terror he named in 9:34, the sense of facing God alone and unrepresented, that part of his prayer already has an answer his did not have.

So here is something to keep this week. The next time your prayers feel too raw, too angry, too honest to be proper, remember you are not required to arbitrate your own case before God. Someone already stands there, one hand toward you, one hand toward the Father, and he is not a stranger like the one at Solferino. He is for you completely. Bring the whole complaint. You already have the mediator Job could only wish for.

articles.title: The Beat No One Had To Start
articles.dek: In a lab dish, a single heart cell keeps its own rhythm with no body around it to ask for one — and buried in Israel's darkest psalm is a doxology that seems to do the very same thing.
articles.quote: The rhythm was written into you long before the ache arrived, and even now, quietly, it is still keeping time.
articles.body:
Take a single heart muscle cell — just one, plucked from tissue and placed alone in a shallow dish of nutrient fluid, with no heart around it, no body, no brain sending it any signal at all. Watch it under a microscope and something strange happens. It contracts. It relaxes. Then, on its own, with nothing outside it and no reason it has to, it contracts again. It keeps going, small and rhythmic, for as long as it's kept alive. Doctors who study the heart have known this for decades: a heart cell doesn't wait to be told when to beat. Deep inside the real thing, a tiny cluster of cells called the sinoatrial node fires off electrical pulses on its own, roughly once a second, whether or not the rest of the body is calm or in crisis. The rhythm isn't a decision made moment by moment. It was built in, at the level of the cell's own chemistry, long before there was ever a body around it to serve.

Keep that image close, because Psalm 89 ends with something almost as strange.

The psalm is credited to a man named Ethan the Ezrahite, and for its first thirty-seven verses it is one of the most soaring celebrations of God's covenant with David found anywhere in Scripture — God's throne "established forever," his faithfulness as sure as "the skies" (Ps 89:2). Then, at verse 38, the floor drops out. "But you have rejected, you have spurned, you have been very angry with your anointed one" (Ps 89:38). The king's crown lies in the dust. The walls meant to protect his people are broken down. Everything God promised David seems, in this moment, to have come apart in real time — and Ethan doesn't pretend otherwise. He says so, plainly, to God's face.

By the time we reach today's verses, that complaint has grown into a full, unguarded cry. "How long, LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?" (Ps 89:46). He asks God to remember how fleeting a human life actually is, how "no one can live and not see death" (Ps 89:48). He reminds God — respectfully, but pointedly — of the love he once swore to David, and asks, in effect, where it has gone (Ps 89:49). He describes the mockery he and his people have carried, the taunts hurled at "the footsteps of your anointed one" (Ps 89:51). And then the psalm simply stops. No angel steps in to answer. No explanation arrives for the disaster. Ethan just runs out of complaint, mid-ache.

And then, one line later, with no transition at all:

Praise be to the LORD forever! Amen and Amen. (Psalm 89:52)

It reads almost like a printing error — as if the wrong ending got pasted onto the wrong psalm. And in a sense, that's not far from true. Scholars have long noticed that the book of Psalms is arranged into five sections, or "books," and each one closes with a short doxology like this, regardless of what comes right before it. Psalm 41 ends one section the same way. So does Psalm 72. So will Psalm 106. Verse 52 isn't really Ethan resolving his own anguish in a single line. It's the ancient editors of the Psalter marking the close of a book, the way you might sign off a letter — and of all the places they could have let that closing stand, they let it stand here, pressed right up against the rawest lament in the entire collection, without softening either one.

It's worth sitting with why no one smoothed that over. It would have been easy enough to move the doxology, or to insert a line first where God answers and Ethan feels better before the "amen" arrives. Instead, the wound and the worship were left touching. The "how long" and the "praise be" sit in the very same breath, unedited, and neither one cancels out the other.

That is the surprise tucked into the last verses of Psalm 89: praise, here, doesn't seem to need an answered prayer as its entry fee. It isn't a reward that only becomes available once your questions are settled. It behaves more like that lone heart cell in the dish — a rhythm placed in God's people before the crisis ever arrived, one that keeps beating quietly even while the crisis is still very much unresolved around it. Ethan didn't need to know how his story would end before he said "Amen." He only needed to still belong to the One he was crying out to in the first place.

This matters for the ordinary Tuesdays we actually live, the ones that never make it into anyone's testimony. Most of us have learned, without quite meaning to, a kind of bargaining faith: I'll praise God once this gets fixed. I'll worship once the test results come back clean, once the money works out, once my son calls me back, once this ache in my chest finally has an explanation. We treat praise as though it belongs at the very end of the story, after the resolution, as if worship is only honest once it's been earned by a happy ending.

Psalm 89 quietly refuses that bargain. It puts the unhealed wound and the doxology on the same page, in the same breath, and lets both be fully true at once. You do not have to stop asking "how long" before you're allowed to say "praise be." You do not have to understand where God has been before you thank him for staying near enough to be shouted at, argued with, and trusted anyway. The heart cell doesn't wait for the whole body to be healthy before it keeps its rhythm going — and the faith planted in you was never designed to wait for a finished story before it beats, either.

So if you're carrying a "how long" tonight — a diagnosis with no clear next step, a marriage that didn't turn out the way you prayed it would, a promise from God that seems to have gone quiet for far too long — you don't need to resolve it before you pray. Say both things honestly, in whatever order they come out of you. Tell God exactly how long it has felt like forever. And somewhere in that very same prayer, let yourself also say amen. Not because the ache is gone. Not because you finally understand. But because the rhythm was written into you long before the ache arrived, and even now, quietly, it is still keeping time.

articles.title: What Kodak Never Went Looking For
articles.dek: When digital photography killed the film industry, one company guarded its old gold and collapsed. Another went searching for something it didn't yet know it had — and Proverbs 8 says that search was never optional.
articles.quote: The fruit of wisdom always outlasts the gold you were chasing instead.
articles.body:
In 1975, an engineer at Eastman Kodak built the world's first digital camera. It weighed eight pounds, took twenty-three seconds to produce a grainy black-and-white image, and it would eventually help kill the company that invented it. Kodak had the technology first — years before anyone else. It also had a wildly profitable film business it wasn't willing to look past. So the invention got shelved, the film cash cow got protected, and Kodak rode that market as long as it could. In 2012, it filed for bankruptcy.

Its longtime Japanese rival, Fujifilm, stared down the exact same collapse in film demand. But Fujifilm's leadership asked a different question: what do we actually, deeply know how to do? Buried in their labs was decades of research into collagen — the protein at the center of every photograph's emulsion layer, and, it turns out, the very protein that keeps human skin firm and elastic. Instead of clutching what was left of their old gold, they went looking, hard, into chemistry nobody thought a camera company would ever need. They found a skincare line, a pharmaceutical division, a materials-science business built on expertise that had been sitting in their labs the whole time, waiting to be sought. Today Fujifilm is a healthcare and technology company worth many times what it was in its film-only years. Same crisis. Same starting chemistry. One company guarded its gold and lost everything. The other went searching for wisdom in an unlikely place and found riches it never expected.

Proverbs 8 pictures wisdom doing something strikingly similar — except she isn't hiding in a lab. She's standing in the street. "Does not wisdom call out? Does not understanding raise her voice?" the chapter opens (Proverbs 8:1). She takes her stand "at the crossroads," "beside the gates leading into the city" (8:2-3) — the busiest, most ordinary places in ancient life. Not a temple. Not a palace. The marketplace, at rush hour. Wisdom isn't whispering to a private few. She is shouting to everyone walking by — merchants, farmers, mothers with kids in tow — because she wants, desperately, to be found.

Then she describes what she's offering, and it isn't modest. "Choose my instruction instead of silver, knowledge rather than choice gold, for wisdom is more precious than rubies," she says a few lines earlier (8:10-11). And then, at the heart of the passage, she gets specific about what actually happens to the person who comes looking.

I love those who love me, and those who seek me find me. With me are riches and honor, enduring wealth and prosperity. My fruit is better than fine gold; what I yield surpasses choice silver. I walk in the way of righteousness, along the paths of justice, bestowing wealth on those who love me and making their treasuries full. (Proverbs 8:17-21, NIV)

Notice the order of that first sentence. It isn't "seek me and you'll get rich." It's "I love those who love me" — first. The seeking that follows isn't a transaction with a vending machine; it's the natural motion of someone already in a relationship. And notice, too, what kind of wealth she promises: not just riches, but enduring wealth. Not just silver, but fruit that surpasses it. This is wisdom insisting that what she gives isn't a substitute for real riches — it is the real riches, the kind that doesn't rust, doesn't get devalued, doesn't vanish the moment the market shifts.

Here's what's easy to miss: Fujifilm didn't get rich by chasing money. They got rich by staying faithful to what they actually knew and loved — their craft, their chemistry — even after the obvious payoff disappeared. They kept seeking before they had any proof it would pay off. That's the part Proverbs 8 keeps insisting on. Wisdom's fruit is always better than fine gold, but you rarely see the fruit while you're still doing the seeking. You only see the gold you're being asked to let go of. The fruit of wisdom always outlasts the gold you were chasing instead — but you have to keep walking toward her before you know that's true.

It's worth noticing where this leads. Centuries after Solomon wrote these words, the apostle Paul would describe Jesus as the one "who has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30). The call from the crossroads in Proverbs 8 — seek me and find me — finds its fullest answer not in a principle to master, but in a person to know. The riches were never just good decisions. They were always meant to lead somewhere, to someone.

So what does seeking wisdom look like on an ordinary Tuesday? It rarely looks dramatic. It looks like opening your Bible before you open your phone. It looks like asking a wiser friend before you make the call. It looks like waiting one more day on a decision instead of grabbing the fast, obvious gold sitting right in front of you. None of that feels like riches in the moment. Fujifilm's scientists didn't know, mid-experiment, that they were building a fortune. They just kept seeking, because the search itself was an act of love for what they knew was true and good.

Pick one decision in front of you this week — small or large, it doesn't matter. Before you reach for the easy gold, ask what wisdom would say. Then do the quieter, less flashy thing: open the Word, ask the question, wait a day. You may not see the fruit yet. But she promised it's already better than the gold you were about to grab. Keep seeking. She wants, more than you know, to be found.
